strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple large-scale datasets (QM9, GEOM-Drugs, B3LYP), with particularly impressive 99.0% validity and 24.2% molecule stability on B3LYP
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including unconditional and class-conditional generation with multiple chemical validity metrics
Sound technical approach combining inertial frame canonicalization for SE(3) invariance with GeoRoPE for geometry-aware attention
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and formal theoretical grounding (Theorem 1)
Extensive supplementary material with detailed proofs and technical exposition
Practical contributions to important problem of 3D molecule generation with demonstrated controllability (83.3% hit rate)
weaknesses: Limited individual technical novelty - inertial frame canonicalization, RoPE-3D, diffusion loss, and classifier-free guidance are all existing techniques; contribution is primarily in their combination

Critical absence of ablation studies on key design choices: no ablation on inertial frame canonicalization, GeoRoPE components separately, hierarchical vs. joint prediction, or block-diagonal structure in attention

Baseline comparison fairness concerns: B3LYP results only compare against EDM and Geo2Seq (others excluded due to 'computational cost'), and Geo2Seq's 73.3% validity vs. InertialAR's 99.0% gap suggests potential implementation issues

Unexplained empirical phenomena: molecule stability metric varies dramatically across datasets (24.2% on B3LYP vs. 0.8% for EDM, but 94.7% vs. 89.4% on QM9), with no discussion of why or whether metrics are consistently computed

Insufficient technical justification for design choices: claim that 'RoPE-3D alone cannot learn adequate information' is unsupported empirical observation; fourth-node selection criteria (largest distance, first quadrant placement) appear arbitrary
Missing analysis of failure modes, edge cases, and scalability: no discussion of symmetric molecules with degenerate eigenvalues, no failure case analysis, no scalability study vs. molecule size
No computational cost analysis: training time, inference time, and memory requirements not reported; anchor point selection for Nystrom approximation not detailed
Insufficient differentiation from concurrent work using inertial frames (Guo et al. 2025, Lu et al. 2025a/b, Cheng et al. 2025b)
Metric reporting inconsistency: abstract claims '7 of 10' SOTA metrics but tables show 8/12 across datasets
Limited reproducibility details: hyperparameter sensitivity not discussed, code availability not mentioned, functional group detection pipeline's 3D→2D→patterns conversion is lossy and error-prone

strengths: Strong empirical results, particularly on large-scale B3LYP (99.3% validity vs 92.9% for EDM), demonstrating scalability beyond small molecule benchmarks
Outstanding controllable generation performance (83.3% average hit rate vs 37-40% for baselines), enabling practical molecular editing
Thorough experimental validation with comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 6-7) and robustness analysis (Section E.1) showing inertial frames are empirically stable
Rigorous theoretical justification with formal Theorem D.1 and proof for the fourth anchor point strategy
Well-motivated hierarchical architecture sensibly decoupling discrete atom types and continuous 3D coordinates via Diffusion Loss, with ablation showing dramatic degradation with L2 regression
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1 overview, Figure 4 molecule editing) and thorough mathematical exposition
Practical contributions enabling efficient variable-length generation and controllable inference via classifier-free guidance
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: primarily combines inertial frame canonicalization (concurrent works Guo et al. 2025, Lu et al. 2025a), standard RDKit reordering, and existing Diffusion Loss (Li et al. 2024a) with incremental improvements

Modest improvements over Geo2Seq on standard benchmarks (QM9: 97.3% vs 97.1% validity; only substantial gain in MolSta at 94.5% vs 93.2%), limiting evidence of practical advantages on smaller datasets

Insufficient ablation studies: missing justification for Manhattan+Euclidean PE concatenation, block-diagonal weight structure (Eq. 12), Nyström vs alternative approximations, and CFG applied to both type/coordinate predictions

Theoretical concerns with SE(3)-invariance claim: method only achieves invariance up to inertial frame choice with residual sign ambiguities; claim that 'our contribution is not theoretically perfect canonicalization' somewhat undermines core premise

Experimental gaps: no error bars/confidence intervals/significance testing, B3LYP limited to only EDM and Geo2Seq baselines (Geo2Seq shows surprisingly poor 73.3% validity raising tuning concerns), MiDi results inconsistently re-evaluated
Missing critical implementation details: hyperparameters (frequency θ₀, Nyström anchor count), training procedures, diffusion step counts, wall-clock time comparisons despite efficiency claims
Generalization unclear: limited to small molecules (≤9 heavy atoms QM9, avg 44 atoms GEOM-Drugs), no per-size performance breakdown, unclear scaling to larger proteins/materials
Limited scope of controllable generation: only simple binary functional group detection rather than complex property-based control (e.g., HOMO-LUMO, solubility); evaluated on only 5 molecule classes
